theme: The Red Sea crossing, redemption through water
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 13:17-14:31. This is the crossing of the Red Sea, the climax of the exodus. Read the story as a drama in three parts: Israel’s fear, God’s promise through Moses, and the crossing itself.
settingTheScene: Israel has left Egypt, with the bones of Joseph carried along as a sign of the promise (13:19). But the journey is not easy. God leads them by a longer route, and then into what looks like a trap, with the sea in front and Pharaoh’s army behind. It is a test of whether they will trust the God who has just rescued them. Everything that follows in Israel’s history, in the Psalms, and in the New Testament, looks back to this moment.
observation: God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, “for God said, Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt” (13:17).
“The LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light” (13:21).
God tells Moses to camp by the sea, so that Pharaoh will think they are wandering confused. “And I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host” (14:4).
Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues with six hundred chariots (14:5-9).
The people cry out in fear and say to Moses, “Is it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?” (14:11).
Moses answers, “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today…The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent” (14:13-14).
The angel of God and the pillar of cloud move between Israel and the Egyptians, bringing darkness to one side and light to the other (14:19-20).

Moses stretches out his hand, a strong east wind drives the sea back, and “the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left” (14:21-22).
The waters return and cover the Egyptians. “Not one of them remained” (14:28).
“Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians…And the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses” (14:30-31).
interpretation:
The first thing to see is that God led them into the trap on purpose. This is not a case of bad navigation. God said, “I will get glory over Pharaoh.” The danger was real, and the people were right to be afraid. But the danger was part of God’s plan to show his power. This is a theme throughout Scripture: God sometimes brings his people to the end of their own resources so that his salvation will be clearly his.

Moses’ answer is the center of the passage, and one of the great statements of faith in the Bible. “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.” There are three commands: do not be afraid, stand still, and watch. This is not a call to passivity in everything, but in this moment there was nothing Israel could do. They were not going to fight their way out. The next line is the promise: “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” The deliverance would be entirely God’s work.

Then notice how God works. He did not remove the sea. He divided it. Israel walked through on dry ground with water on each side. The very thing that seemed to be their death, the sea, became their path. And the same sea became the Egyptians’ grave. The same event is salvation for one people and judgment for another.

The last verses tell you what the miracle accomplished in the hearts of the people. They “feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.” Redemption produced faith. We saw in Psalm 106 that the faith did not last, but at that moment it was real.

For the New Testament writers, the crossing of the sea is a picture of baptism. Paul says that “all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2). Passing through the water means leaving the old master behind and belonging to a new leader. It also looks to the cross, where Christ, the greater Moses, passes through the waters of judgment so that his people can walk through on dry ground.
connection: Isaiah 43:2 says, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.” Paul compares the crossing to baptism in 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. Peter says that “baptism…now saves you” as an appeal to God for a good conscience (1 Peter 3:21), after speaking of the flood. Revelation 15:3 describes the saints singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God.”
application:
Think of a place where you feel hemmed in, with the sea in front and an enemy behind. Say aloud, “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.”

Take a few minutes of true silence in prayer this week. Resist the urge to fix the situation, and watch for God’s salvation.

Remember your baptism, if you have been baptized. If you have not, ask what it would mean to take that step.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you fear when you face a sea you cannot cross.
Ask him to fight for you and to teach you to be still.
Thank him for the salvation he worked in Christ.
